stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
In a survey of 140 highway bridges, engineers found that decks treated with a silane sealant showed roughly half as much surface cracking after fifteen years as untreated decks. The team concluded that the sealant substantially slows deck deterioration and recommended applying it statewide.

Text 2
The survey's crack counts are not in question. However, the sealed decks were mostly built after 2005, under stricter concrete-mix standards, and many sit on rural routes with light truck traffic. Newer concrete and gentler loads could have produced the same difference, so the sealant's role remains unestablished.
choices: The sealant was the main reason the sealed decks developed less cracking.
The sealant does nothing to slow the deterioration of concrete decks.
Sealed decks in the survey cracked less than untreated decks did.
Decks built before 2005 should be replaced rather than sealed.
explanation: Text 1 reports that sealed decks showed about half as much cracking, and Text 2 opens by accepting those counts ('not in question') before disputing the cause. The two authors agree on the observation, and they split only over the explanation for it.

A.why: You picked Text 1's conclusion. Text 2 says newer concrete and lighter traffic could explain the difference, and it calls the sealant's role 'unestablished,' so the author of Text 2 would not accept this.

B.why: You read Text 2 as proving the sealant useless. Text 2 argues only that the survey doesn't show the sealant works. That is a claim about missing evidence, not proof that the sealant has no effect, and Text 1 plainly rejects it.

D.why: You latched onto the 2005 date in Text 2. Neither author makes any recommendation about replacing older decks.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Fossil leaves from a 56-million-year-old site in Wyoming bear unusually many insect feeding scars. Because the site dates to a brief interval of rapid global warming, paleobotanist Lena Ortiz argues that higher temperatures drove a surge in insect herbivory.

Text 2
Ortiz's damage tallies are careful, and the warm interval is well dated. But most of her leaves come from a single ancient riverbank, where fast-growing, thin-leaved plants dominated. Such plants are eaten heavily in any climate, so the scars may reflect which species happened to fossilize there rather than the warming itself.
choices: The Wyoming leaves show an unusually high level of insect feeding damage.
Rising temperatures caused the increase in insect feeding at the Wyoming site.
Temperature has no effect on how heavily insects feed on plants.
The Wyoming site is too poorly dated to be linked to the warming.
explanation: Text 1 reports unusually many feeding scars, and Text 2 calls Ortiz's damage tallies 'careful.' Both accept how much damage there is. Text 2 disputes only whether warming caused it.

B.why: This is Ortiz's conclusion, and it is the claim Text 2 is written to reject. Text 2 says the scars may reflect which plant species fossilized at the site rather than the warming.

C.why: You made Text 2 stronger than it is. Text 2 says the damage at this site may have another explanation. It never claims that temperature has no effect on herbivory in general.

D.why: Text 2 explicitly grants that 'the warm interval is well dated,' so neither author questions the site's age.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Manuscript copies of a set of 1720s violin sonatas carry performers' pencil markings that lengthen certain notes. Musicologist Dara Feld concludes that musicians of the period routinely played uneven rhythms even where the notation was even, and that modern performers should do the same.

Text 2
The markings Feld catalogued are real and revealing. Yet nearly all appear in copies owned by a single court orchestra in Dresden, whose director was known for his idiosyncratic taste. What one ensemble did is not necessarily what musicians across Europe did.
choices: Musicians across Europe routinely played uneven rhythms in this period.
Performers outside Dresden played these sonatas exactly as written.
Modern performers should play these sonatas with strictly even rhythms.
The pencil markings show that some performers lengthened certain notes.
explanation: Text 2 calls the markings 'real and revealing,' so it accepts that at least the Dresden players lengthened notes. It does not accept that this practice was routine everywhere. Both authors agree that some performers lengthened notes, and they disagree about how widespread the practice was.

A.why: This is Feld's broad conclusion, and it is the claim Text 2 narrows. Text 2 argues that one ensemble's habits don't show what musicians across Europe did.

B.why: You treated 'not shown' as 'shown false.' Text 2 says only that the Dresden evidence can't speak for other musicians. It offers no evidence about how anyone outside Dresden played.

C.why: Text 1 recommends that modern performers use uneven rhythms, and Text 2 says nothing about modern performance. You aimed Text 2's doubt at a part of Text 1 it never addresses.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
On test plots in Iowa, fields planted with a winter rye cover crop yielded 8 percent more soybeans the following summer than fields left bare. Agronomist Priya Nair concluded that rye cover crops raise soybean yields and urged farmers across the Midwest to adopt them.

Text 2
Nair's plots did produce more soybeans. That trial, however, ran during two unusually dry summers, when rye's mulch helps soil hold moisture. In wetter years, other trials have found that rye can delay spring soil warming and slightly reduce yields, so the benefit may hold only under drought.
choices: Rye cover crops raise soybean yields in Midwest fields in most years.
Rye plots in Nair's dry-summer trial yielded more soybeans than bare plots.
Rye cover crops lower soybean yields in all but the driest years.
Soil temperature matters more to soybeans than soil moisture does.
explanation: Text 2 grants the result directly: 'Nair's plots did produce more soybeans.' Where it parts from Text 1 is scope, since the gain may hold only in drought years like those of the trial. Both authors therefore accept the trial's result.

A.why: This is Nair's general conclusion. Text 2 limits it by saying the benefit may appear only in dry years, so it would not grant that rye helps in most years.

C.why: You turned Text 2's hedges ('can,' 'slightly,' 'may') into a firm rule. Text 1 would reject this claim in any case, because Nair found that rye raised yields.

D.why: Text 2 mentions both soil temperature and soil moisture, but neither author ranks one above the other.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
After a city installed reflective white roofing on 3,000 buildings, summer afternoon temperatures downtown averaged 0.9°C lower than in the previous five summers. The city's climate office concluded that the roofing program had cooled the downtown area.

Text 2
Downtown was indeed cooler over that period. But the same summers were cooler across the entire region, including rural stations far from any new roofs, because of a persistent shift in the jet stream. Unless the downtown drop exceeded the regional one, the roofs cannot be credited with it.
choices: The reflective roofing was responsible for the cooler downtown afternoons.
Reflective roofing does not lower temperatures in city centers.
The regional cooling was confined to areas near the new roofs.
Downtown summer afternoons were cooler after the roofing program began.
explanation: Text 2 opens with 'Downtown was indeed cooler,' which accepts the temperature drop that Text 1 reports. Text 2 then offers a different cause, a regional jet-stream shift. The cooling itself is the common ground.

A.why: This is the climate office's conclusion, and Text 2 rejects it. Text 2 says the roofs can't be credited unless downtown cooled more than the region as a whole.

B.why: You picked the 'proves the opposite' version. Text 2 says only that this record doesn't show the roofs worked. It makes no general claim that reflective roofs can't cool cities.

C.why: Text 2 says the cooling reached 'rural stations far from any new roofs,' which is the opposite of this statement.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Banding records show that American robins in a Minnesota study area now arrive in spring about twelve days earlier than they did in 1980. Ornithologist Sam Okafor concludes that the birds have evolved to migrate earlier in response to warming winters.

Text 2
Okafor's arrival dates are solid. His explanation, though, is premature. Robins adjust their pace to the weather they meet along the way, and an individual bird can shift its timing from one year to the next. Earlier arrivals may therefore reflect flexible behavior rather than any inherited change.
choices: The robins' earlier arrival reflects an inherited change in timing.
Robins now reach the study area earlier in spring than in 1980.
Warming winters have had no influence on when the robins arrive.
An individual robin keeps the same migration schedule from year to year.
explanation: Text 2 calls Okafor's arrival dates 'solid' and calls only his explanation 'premature.' Both authors accept that the robins arrive earlier. They disagree over whether evolution or flexible behavior explains it.

A.why: This is Okafor's evolutionary conclusion, which Text 2 calls premature because flexible behavior could explain the same arrival dates.

C.why: You made Text 2 deny any role for climate. Text 2 actually says robins respond to the weather they meet, so it never claims warming has no influence, and Text 1 would reject this statement outright.

D.why: Text 2 states that an individual bird 'can shift its timing from one year to the next,' so this reverses what Text 2 says.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Divers surveying a Caribbean reef counted 40 percent more juvenile parrotfish inside a newly protected zone than in fished waters nearby, just three years after fishing was banned there. The researchers concluded that the ban had allowed the parrotfish population to rebound.

Text 2
The survey found more juveniles inside the zone—that much is clear. Yet the zone was drawn around the reef's densest seagrass beds, which parrotfish larvae favor when they settle. The zone may simply have held more juveniles all along; without counts from before the ban, a rebound has not been shown.
choices: More juvenile parrotfish were counted inside the zone than outside it.
The fishing ban allowed the zone's parrotfish population to rebound.
The fishing ban has done nothing to help the reef's parrotfish.
Parrotfish larvae tend to avoid seagrass beds when they settle.
explanation: Text 2 grants the survey result ('that much is clear') and then argues that the difference may have existed before the ban. Both authors accept the higher count inside the zone.

B.why: This is Text 1's conclusion. Text 2 says that without counts from before the ban, a rebound 'has not been shown.'

C.why: You mistook 'not shown' for 'disproved.' Text 2 says the evidence is missing. It never says the ban failed.

D.why: Text 2 says larvae favor seagrass beds when they settle, which is the reverse of this statement.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
A 1507 world map held in a private archive shows a narrow strait at the southern tip of South America, thirteen years before Magellan's crew sailed through one. Historian Elise Marrow argues that the mapmaker must have drawn on reports from an earlier, unrecorded voyage to the region.

Text 2
Marrow is right that the strait appears on the map, and the map's date is secure. Mapmakers of the era, however, often drew speculative channels where they believed one ought to exist, since a westward passage was eagerly sought. The strait could be a lucky guess rather than a record of anyone's voyage.
choices: The mapmaker drew on reports from an earlier voyage to the region.
The map was most likely drawn after Magellan's voyage.
The 1507 map shows a strait at South America's southern tip.
No European ship reached the region before Magellan's crew did.
explanation: Text 2 states that 'Marrow is right that the strait appears on the map.' Both authors accept what the map shows. Text 2 disputes only Marrow's claim that the strait records a real voyage.

A.why: This is Marrow's conclusion. Text 2 suggests the strait could be a speculative guess, so it would not agree.

B.why: Text 2 grants that 'the map's date is secure,' so neither author doubts that the map predates Magellan.

D.why: You read Text 2 as ruling out an earlier voyage. Text 2 says only that the map doesn't prove one happened. It makes no claim that no such voyage took place.
